Goal: write node:test tests for changes in /root/bench-runs/h5-a984a158 (small Node 24 HTTP expense-sharing service, no dependencies; do NOT npm install anything; only Node built-ins). Do not change lib/ or server.mjs or README.md; only add/edit files under test/. `npm test` runs `node --test "test/*.test.mjs"`, so new files must be test/*.test.mjs. Use test/helpers.mjs (withApp, startApp, tempDataFile) — tests reach the import over HTTP only.

Changes to cover:
1. Bug fix in lib/validate.mjs parseAmount: Math.round instead of Math.trunc (4.35 was stored as 434 cents → shown 4.34). Test: POST expense amount 4.35 shows 4.35 in the reply and in GET list; also other values like 0.29, 1.13, 8.2, 1000000, 0.01 (a plausible wrong impl e.g. trunc or toFixed must fail).
2. Bug fix in lib/ledger.mjs splitEvenly: leftover cents go one each to the FIRST people in split, so shares add to the amount. 10.00 among Ann, Ben, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33; balances after Ann pays 10 for all three: Ann 6.66, Ben -3.33, Cara -3.33 (sum 0). Test split order matters (split ['Cara','Ann','Ben'] → Cara gets the extra cent), and 2 leftover cents (e.g. 0.05 among 3 → 2,2,1 cents). Update test/ledger.test.mjs unit tests for splitEvenly too.
3. New endpoint POST /groups/:id/import in lib/import.mjs (routed in lib/routes.mjs). The spec is in README.md section "## Import" — read it AND the full spec below, and probe every line with a test a plausible wrong implementation would fail. Full spec:
- Body `{"entries": [...], "dry_run": <boolean>, "skip_recorded": <boolean>}`; flags optional (default false). Entry = expense `{"type":"expense", description, payer, amount, split?}` or payment `{"type":"payment", from, to, amount}`; each field same rule as on POST expenses/payments. A field is left out only when its key is absent: present key is checked whatever its value, null included (`"dry_run": null` → 400 `dry_run must be true or false`; `"split": null` → bad-split).
- Body >10KB → 413; non-object body → 400. Then in order: (1) unknown group → 404 {"error":"not found"} (even if body is otherwise bad, e.g. unknown field); (2) 400 {"error": msg} first of: `unknown field <name>` (first unknown in Object.keys order), `entries must be an array of 1 to 50 items` (0 and 51 fail, 1 and 50 pass; non-array fails), `dry_run must be true or false`, `skip_recorded must be true or false` (e.g. "true" string, 1, null fail).
- (3) 422 {"error":"import rejected","problems":[{index, rule}...]} sorted by index, one per bad entry, first rule broken in order: not-an-object (null, array, number, string), bad-type, unknown-field (expense takes type, description, payer, amount, split; payment takes type, from, to, amount — e.g. expense with `from` is unknown-field; unknown-field beats bad-description), expense: bad-description, bad-payer, bad-amount, bad-split; then duplicate (an earlier entry that broke none of not-an-object..bad-split is an expense with same payer, amount (cents) and description after trim().toLowerCase(); split not compared), then already-recorded (group already has expense with same payer/amount/description; expenses of OTHER groups don't count). Earlier entry counts for duplicate even when it's itself duplicate/already-recorded, skipped or not. Example: two identical entries both matching an existing expense → skip_recorded true: problems [{index:1, rule:"duplicate"}]; false: [{index:0,"already-recorded"},{index:1,"duplicate"}]. Payment: bad-from (not member), bad-to (not member or equals from), bad-amount. Payments never duplicate/already-recorded: identical payments all imported. An invalid earlier expense (e.g. bad-split) does NOT make a later identical valid one a duplicate. Amount 4.35 vs 4.350? (same cents) → duplicate; "Taxi" vs "  taxi " → duplicate; different payer → not duplicate.
- skip_recorded true: entry whose first broken rule is already-recorded is skipped, not a problem. All-skipped import succeeds: 201 (200 with dry_run) with expenses [], payments [], skipped all indexes, current balances, and writes nothing to the data file (check file bytes/mtime unchanged, or file absent stays absent… note the group creation writes the file, so compare content before/after).
- 422 and 400 save nothing (check GET expenses/payments and that next POST id is unchanged).
- Success 201 {"expenses","payments","skipped","balances"}: expense/payment shapes exactly as POST replies (expense {id,description,payer,amount,split,shares}, payment {id,from,to,amount}); ids consecutive per kind in entry order starting at next id the POST route would give (ids are global across groups and never reused — test after a delete and with another group's expenses). Example: entries [expense, skipped expense, payment, expense] with next ids E, P → expenses get E, E+1, payment P; after, next ids E+2, P+1. skipped ascending; [] when none. balances = map like GET balances's `balances` value (not nested), all members in group order, after the import. One write: data survives restart (startApp on same file).
- dry_run true: same checks/errors, success → same body with 200, nothing saved; ids are those a real import would get; next real POST gets the first of them.

Done means: new test file(s) (e.g. test/import.test.mjs) plus fix-tests, `npm test` fully green, each spec line above has a test. If a test reveals an implementation bug in lib/import.mjs, do not fix lib code — report it with the failing case in your REPORT (Status: blocked, listing the bug). Run your own reviewer gate on your test files.
Skills for this job: none needed.
Awake builder sections: none (supervisor `main` built the code).
End with your REPORT block.

## What NOT to save in memory

- Code patterns, conventions, architecture, file paths, or project structure — these can be derived by reading the current project state.
- Git history, recent changes, or who-changed-what — `git log` / `git blame` are authoritative.
- Debugging solutions or fix recipes — the fix is in the code; the commit message has the context.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a PR list or activity summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:
  type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

- Since this memory is local-scope (not checked into version control), tailor your memories to this project and machine

- **Import:** each rule has a test that a plausible wrong version would fail. That covers the order of the checks, null values, duplicates against already-recorded expenses, ids across groups after a delete, the all-skipped import not touching the data file, dry runs, and data surviving a restart.

**Not checked by running:** I couldn't run deliberately broken copies of the code, because the permission system blocked copying the project to /tmp and two of the helpers couldn't run commands at all. Instead I checked by reading the tests that each likely wrong version (truncating, `trimEnd`, null flags treated as absent, ids taken from a count, writing when everything is skipped, a dry run that saves) has an assertion that would fail.

The reviewer passed the tests at 8/10 with no fix rounds needed. I then added the four tests it found missing: payer and split in the already-recorded check, amounts compared in cents, and a payment that matches one already recorded.
